description: We are building Desypher, an Earth system trend detective. Pick any spot on the globe, choose a measurement and years, and see whether that place is really changing: quantified trends with uncertainty, NASA satellite imagery, and a plain-language verdict you can download as an evidence card. Our interest is making Earth observation usable without code - turning live NASA data and statistical tests into clear local answers. We build full-stack apps across Python backends and modern web frontends.
summary:
deSypher is a free, browser-based Earth System Trend Detective that helps people investigate environmental change without writing code. Users choose a location, measurement and time period, then explore NASA POWER records through charts, statistical trend tests, confidence ranges and plain-language explanations.

We address the challenge by turning Earth observations into evidence people can question and use. A second-source check against ECMWF ERA5 shows where datasets agree or disagree, while NASA GIBS imagery adds visual context without treating pictures as proof of a trend. Users can download evidence cards and save investigations for later.

Our focus is accessibility for student projects, teaching and research. deSypher makes the size of a trend and its uncertainty visible, including when the evidence does not support a significant change. It also explains that coarse climate grids cannot describe conditions at an individual street or farm. This helps users work with real NASA data while avoiding confident claims the data cannot justify.
details:
Earth data is open. The ability to investigate it is not equally accessible. deSypher closes that gap by turning a local question, "Is it really changing where I live?", into an investigation that students, educators and early-stage researchers can carry out without writing code.

HOW IT WORKS

Users select a point or region, a measurement and a time period. deSypher retrieves NASA POWER time-series data and sends it to a Python analysis backend. It combines Mann-Kendall analysis and Sen's slope, seasonal Mann-Kendall, and autocorrelation-adjusted regression to examine the direction, rate and statistical significance of change. Results include a trend estimate, a 95% confidence range and a plain-language verdict. Agreement between these complementary tests is a robustness check on the same record, not three independent sources of evidence.

Users can examine annual values and warming stripes, compare before-and-after NASA GIBS/MODIS imagery, and check supported measurements against ECMWF ERA5 through Open-Meteo. A downloadable evidence card and saved investigation notebook help carry findings into projects and reports instead of leaving them inside a dashboard. The notebook can also recheck saved investigations as later data becomes available.

WHAT MAKES IT DIFFERENT

The creative idea is a detective's workflow: ask a question, inspect evidence, challenge the finding and keep a record. Images provide context; statistical tests provide the trend evidence. A second dataset can expose disagreement rather than merely reinforce the first answer.

Most importantly, deSypher does not force every investigation into a dramatic story. In working temperature examples for 1981-2025, the selected Svalbard grid cell shows a significant increase across all three tests, while the selected Bhubaneswar grid cell reaches significance in none. The latter is reported as insufficient evidence of a trend in that record, not proof that the place is unaffected by climate change. Learning when the evidence does not justify a conclusion is part of the product's value.

TOOLS AND DEVELOPMENT

The browser interface uses JavaScript, React and React Native Web/Expo, with a Python statistics backend. The frontend is hosted on Cloudflare Pages and the backend on Render. NASA POWER drives the climate analysis; NASA GIBS/MODIS supplies imagery. A separate greenness view integrates MODIS NDVI through Microsoft Planetary Computer. The system uses web services rather than custom sensing hardware, and users need no specialist software installation or account.

BENEFITS, IMPACT AND DESIGN CHOICES

Our intended impact is to make NASA data usable in classroom investigations, student projects and exploratory research, while teaching people to question environmental claims. We prioritized low-cost access, readable explanations, visible uncertainty and reusable evidence over a display of unexplained charts.

Scientific transparency shaped our design. deSypher shows the selected location, time period and confidence range so users can judge what each result supports. It distinguishes grid-scale patterns from conditions at an individual street or farm, measured trends from their causes, and visual context from statistical evidence. These choices help users build stronger projects and research questions while recognizing when a finding needs closer investigation.

CONCLUSION

Our goal is to make open Earth data usable, not simply visible. By bringing NASA records, statistical testing and clear explanations into one accessible workflow, we help students and researchers move from a question to evidence they can examine and reuse. Success means making a finding easier to reach without making it easier to overstate.

Choose a place. Test the change. Keep uncertainty visible.
